quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "express" ends in /s/ and "yourself" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /s/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "express yourself", /s/ + /j/ becomes /ʃ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "find time" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /d/ in "find" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /d/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "find time", the /d/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /t/ and /j/ separately between "best" and "year", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /t/ and /j/ combine into /tʃ/ in "best year".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "hot" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the velar sound in "game"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a velar position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /k/ in "hot game".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "hot". With a bilabial consonant starting "meal" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /t/ ending "hot" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /t/ becomes /p/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "meal".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "lost" and "luggage". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /t/ in "lost luggage" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "seven balloons" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /n/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /n/ rarely stays /n/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /m/, which is exactly what you hear in "seven balloons".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /t/ at the end of "collect". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "data"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /t/ at the end of "collect" disappears before the consonant that starts "data".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "first night" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /t/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "first night", the /t/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "miss your" quickly and casually. The /s/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /s/ and /j/ into /ʃ/. That's why "miss your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "last" meets "chance" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "last chance" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "this" and "young": /s/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /s/ and /j/ become /ʃ/ in "this young" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "guess"'s velar sound before it even finishes "good". What happens to /d/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /d/ to /g/ at the end of "good" happens because the following velar consonant in "guess" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two consonants become one here. Focus on where "first" ends and "year" begins — what's the resulting blended sound?
quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /t/ meets a "you"-type word. In "first year", the result is /tʃ/, not /t/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Rather than pronouncing /z/ then /j/ separately, fluent speakers coalesce them. What do you actually hear in "please yourself"?
quests.explanation: Notice that neither the original /z/ nor /j/ survives on its own — they combine into /ʒ/. That fusion is what makes "please yourself" sound natural and fast.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "slept" get pronounced before "late", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "slept" is the one that goes missing before "late".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen at natural speed: does "not yet" keep two distinct consonant sounds at the boundary, or blend them into a new one?
quests.explanation: In relaxed, natural speech, /t/ and /j/ rarely stay separate at a word boundary like this one. They coalesce into /tʃ/, exactly as in "not yet".
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "wide" and "bridge" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /d/ ending "wide" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "bridge", surfacing as /b/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "front desk" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /t/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "front desk".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "trend" is trapped between two other consonants right before "now". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /d/ from "trend" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "now".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "flat" — it's still there, just different. What does /t/ turn into before the velar sound in "ground"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /t/ ending "flat" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /k/ to match the velar sound beginning "ground".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ at the end of "great" is about to meet a velar sound in "game". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a velar consonant, /t/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "great game", /t/ becomes /k/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "sound" and the /j/ starting "your" don't survive as separate sounds in fast speech. What do they turn into together?
quests.explanation: This is why "sound your" doesn't sound like two crisp, separate words: the boundary consonant /d/ and the /j/ of "your" merge into the single sound /dʒ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a sound-merging boundary. What new consonant replaces /s/ + /j/ when you say "this yacht" naturally?
quests.explanation: Coalescence is a genuine sound change, not just fast talking — /s/ plus /j/ reliably becomes /ʃ/ in phrases like "this yacht" across natural English speech.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "good cook" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /d/ stay a /d/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /d/ ending "good" turns into /g/ because "cook" begins with a velar consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "girl". What does that do to the /d/ just before it in "good"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /d/ anticipate the velar sound ahead. So in "good girl", /d/ is pronounced as /g/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /d/ ending "bad" to the bilabial sound that opens "mood". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /d/ becomes /b/ in "bad mood" to match the bilabial consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "bad" to "pain". Is it still /d/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /d/ meets a bilabial sound, the /d/ shifts to /b/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "bad pain".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "great" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the velar sound in "cook"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a velar position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /k/ in "great cook".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try blending "expand" straight into "your" without a pause. The /d/ and /j/ fuse — into what sound?
quests.explanation: The two sounds don't just sit next to each other; they blend into /dʒ/. That's the defining feature of coalescence, and it's exactly what happens in "expand your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".
